Every age has its orthodoxy, and the strangest thing about it is how invisible it seems to those inside it. We do not think of our assumptions as assumptions; we think of them as common sense. It is only when a stranger arrives and asks why we do what we do that the habit is exposed. The man who defends tradition is often accused of lacking imagination, but I suspect the opposite: it takes a livelier imagination to see that the world might have been otherwise, and still to say that this arrangement has merits. Heresy, in the end, is a kind of loyalty to a different truth, and the heretic is rarely as lonely as he looks.
